Choline chloride and ethylene glycol based deep eutectic solvent (DES) *versus* hydroxyl functionalized room temperature ionic liquids (RTILs): assessing the differences in microscopic behaviour between the DES and RTILs†
Sahadev Barik, ID ^ab Manjari Chakraborty, ID ^ab Amita Mahapatra ID ^ab and Moloy Sarkar ID ^*ab

With the aim of understanding the differences in the behavior of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) and room temperature ionic liquids (RTILs) in terms of their structure, dynamics, and intra- and intermolecular interactions, three different ILs and one DES having similar functionalities (hydroxyl) have been investigated by using both ensembled average and single-molecule spectroscopic techniques. Specifically, for this purpose, a choline chloride based DES (ethaline) and three hydroxyl functionalized ILs (1-(2-hydroxyethyl)-3-imidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHEMIM][NTF2]), N-(2-hydroxyl ethyl)-N-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHEMPY][NTf2]), and N-(2-hydroxyethyl)- N,N-dimethylpropan-1-aminium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHC3CH][NTf2])) are employed and investigated by EPR, time-resolved fluorescence, NMR and FCS studies. Estimation of polarity through EPR spectroscopy has revealed that the hydroxyl ILs employed in these studies are hyper-polar (close to water) in nature, whereas the polarity of the DES is found to be close to those of aliphatic polyhydroxy-alcohols. Interestingly, both time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy and FCS studies on these systems have suggested that the hydroxyl ILs are more dynamically heterogeneous than the DES. More interestingly, PFG-NMR measurements have indicated that the fluid structure of ethaline is relatively more associated as compared to those of the ILs despite the fact that all the cations have the same hydroxyl functionalities. All these investigations have essentially demonstrated that, despite having similar functionalities, both the DES and hydroxyl ILs employed in the present study exhibit microscopic behaviours that are significantly different from each other, indicating the interplay of various intermolecular interactions within the constituent species in governing the behaviours of these solvent systems.

coulombic interaction between the cations and anions is the dominant contributor to the structures and properties of the ILs.12,13 However, in the case of DESs, it is believed that complex hydrogen bonding between the constituent species is responsible for governing the macroscopic physicochemical properties of DESs.7-9 Due to this it has also been pointed out that there are much more differences than similarities between these two classes of systems.10,11,14 In this scenario, it would be interesting to know the comparative behavior of both DESs and ILs having similar functionalities (hydroxyl group) so as to understand whether the microscopic behavior of these classes of solvent systems is dictated by hydrogen bonding interaction or other types of intermolecular interactions.

RTILs are salts with low melting points which entirely consist of ions and are liquids at room temperature. 1,2,12 Since there are numerous possible combinations of cations and anions, many ILs can be prepared as per the need of the end-user, and because of this, these solvents are termed 'designer solvents'. 2,12 With increase in chemical variety among ILs, they are further classified into task specific ILs, functionalized ILs, protic ILs and poly-ionic ILs. 15-17 In contrast to ILs, DESs are usually prepared by the combination of hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), which results in a significant decrease in the freezing point temperature owing to the extensive interspecies hydrogen bonding network. 7-9,18 The most common HBA are usually ammonium and phosphonium salts, whereas HBD are usually alcohols, amides and acid functionalities. 7-9 Since the starting materials for the preparation of DESs are relatively cheaper as compared to ILs, large scale preparation of DESs is possible for their use in various fields such as electrochemistry, 19,20 synthesis, 21 catalysis, 18,22 nanotechnology, 23,24 and gas adsorption. 25

Some notable experimental techniques like fluorescence, 26-32 small angle neutron scattering, 33,34 NMR diffusion 35-39 and theo- retical studies based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulation 40-45 have been used to explore the microscopic structural organisation and dynamics of DESs and RTILs independently. Atkins and co-workers 17 suggested that ILs have huge structural diversity depending on the nature of ions as well as their self- organisation into ion pairs, ions' crystal lattice, H-bonding network and micellar domains. Fayer and co-workers 46 also reported that the intra- and intermolecular interactions in ILs have significant impact on the heterogeneous microstructural organisation and liquid morphology which contribute to the dynamic heterogeneity of ILs. Moreover, the complex solvation processes of ILs have also been reported by many groups and it has been demonstrated that the multiple time scales of solvent relaxation phenomena are significantly affected by the hetero- geneity of the medium. 47-49 However, for DESs the assessment of the heterogeneity of the medium is not straightforward. For example, Biswas and co-workers 32,50,51 have reported that the non-ionic DES formed by the combination of acetamide and urea is not heterogeneous, whereas the choline chloride/urea combination or acetamide/electrolyte mixture are both spatially and dynamically heterogenous. Furthermore, the DES ethaline, a mixture of choline chloride and ethylene glycol, is reported to

be spatially homogeneous but dynamically heterogeneous. 52,53 Though there are a few studies which describe the structural organisation of some neat ILs and DESs, the understanding about the differences in microscopic structural organisation between these two classes of substances still remains hazy. Therefore, it would be interesting to probe the differences in microscopic behaviour between DESs and ILs in terms of the nature of solute-solvent interaction, intermolecular interaction and dynamics of the solvent systems by employing DESs and ILs having similar functional moieties. Studies on this aspect are expected to be helpful in understanding the structure- property relationship for these classes of substances (DESs and RTILs).

In light of the foregoing discussion, the current study focuses on the understanding of differences in microscopic behaviour between DESs and ionic liquids. For this purpose, a DES, namely ethaline (choline chloride + ethylene glycol 1:2 ratio), and three other hydroxyl group containing room temperature ionic liquids are employed for the study. The hydroxyl group based ILs have been chosen purposefully so that apart from the role of the hydroxyl group, various other factors which account for the microscopic behaviour of both DES and ILs can be clearly understood. Furthermore, for a fair comparison between the DES and ionic liquids, a cholinium ionic liquid ([OHC3CH][NTf2]) (Chart 1) consisting of the propyl chain has also been used for this study. The differences in microscopic behaviour between the DES and hydroxyl ILs have been investigated with the help of different spectroscopic techniques such as steady state and time resolved fluorescence spectroscopy, fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy so that information regarding the local environment, the solute-solvent interaction and the dynamics of the solvent systems can be obtained. Especially, the rotational and translational diffusion dynamics of some selected probes determined through time resolved fluorescence anisotropy measurement and FCS techniques, respectively,

All these investigations have revealed significant differences in microscopic behaviours between two ILs and the DES despite the fact that they have the same (hydroxyl) functionalities. ## 2. Experimental ### 2.1. Materials Ethylene glycol, 1-methylimidazole, N-methylpyrrolidine, N,N-dimethylethanolamine, 1-bromopropane, Coumarin (153), perylene, 8-methoxypyrene-1,3,6-trisulfonic acid trisodium salt (MPTS), and 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Choline chloride and lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiNTf₂) were received from TCI. 1-(2-Hydroxyethyl)-3-imidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide was purchased from io-li-tec. 2-Chloroethanol was purchased from HiMedia. All the chemicals were dried under vacuum and used without any further purification. DMSO-d⁶ from Sigma Aldrich was used as solvent for recording NMR. The molecular structures of the components of the DES, hydroxyl ILs and different probe molecules used in this study are provided in Chart 1. The details regarding the synthesis, characterization, water content and sample preparation are provided in the ESI.†

## 2.2. Instrumentation The absorption spectra of the samples were collected using a Cary 100 biospectrophotometer. A Cary Eclipse fluorescence (Agilent Technologies) spectrophotometer was used for recording the steady state fluorescence spectra of the samples. A time correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) spectrometer (OB 920) was used for the measurements of time resolved fluorescence anisotropy with the help of a 405 nm picosecond diode laser (EPL) as an excitation source. A dilute solution of Ludox in water was taken as a scatterer to obtain the instrument response function (IRF) and it was found to be around 80 ps for the 405 nm laser. Fluorescence intensities for parallel (||) and perpendicular (⊥) polarization were collected alternatively until a peak difference between the parallel (||) and perpendicular (⊥) decays of ~5000 (at _t_ = 0) was observed. The same procedure was applied for _G_-factor calculation but with horizontal polarization of the exciting laser beam and 5 cycles of repetition. The temperature of the cell was monitored by circulating water through the cell holder using a Quantum along with a North West (TC 125) temperature controller. A Hamamatsu microchannel plate photomultiplier tube (R3809U-50) detector was used to collect the decay signals of

the samples. The decay curves were analysed with the help of F980 decay analysis software. The decay curves were fitted through non-linear least squares iteration methods and the quality of the fitting was judged from the chi-square (x²) values as well as by verifying the weight deviation. The viscosities of all the samples were measured using an LVDV-III Ultra Brookfield Cone and Plate viscometer (experimental error: ±2%). A Bruker Super QCW-EPR bridge (model A300) X band spectrometer was used for recording the EPR spectra and WinEPR SymFonia software (version 1.26 beta) was used for simulation of the EPR spectra. All the NMR measurements were carried out on a 9.4 T Bruker Avance NMR spectrometer with 400.1 MHz Larmor frequencies for H¹.

For FCS measurements, a time-resolved confocal fluores-cence setup (MicroTime 200, PicoQuant), equipped with an inverted microscope (Olympus IX 71) along with a water immersion objective (Olympus UPlanSApo NA 1.2, 60x), was used. The excitation source was a pulsed diode laser (403 nm) with an FWHM of 176 ps and a repetition rate of 20 MHz. The laser beam was made to pass through a polarization maintain-ing single-mode optical fiber and focused onto the sample (which was placed on a coverslip) using a water immersion objective which was also used to collect the fluorescence light emitted from the samples. The emitted beam was then filtered by using a 425 nm filter to remove any excitation light. The signal was then focused onto a 50 µm diameter pinhole to remove the out-of-focus signal, recollimated, and directed onto a (50/50) beam splitter prior to entering two single-photon avalanche photodiodes (SPADs). The signals from the two SPAD detectors were cross-correlated to generate fluorescence corre-lation traces. A SymPhoTime software controlled PicoHarp300 TCSPC module was used for data acquisition in a time-tagged time-resolved (TTTR) mode. All FCS experiments were carried out at room temperature (~298 K). During all FCS measure-ments, the excitation power was kept at ~4 µW. The excitation power was kept low during all FCS studies so as to avoid the contribution of background noise. The absorption and emis-sion spectra as well as the plots of fluorescence intensity time traces for both neat solvents and the probe molecules are provided in Fig. S1 and S2 (ESI†) to demonstrate the optical cleanness of the concerned media.

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Steady state spectral measurements The steady state absorption and emission spectra of a dipolar probe, C153, in both the DES and hydroxyl functionalized ILs (hydroxyl ILs) are provided in Fig. 1. The absorption and emission maxima of C153 in all the concerned solvents are given in Table 1. From Fig. 1, one can observe that there are hardly any differences observed in the emission or absorption spectra of C153 in the DES and hydroxyl ILs. From Table 1 also no noticeable changes in absorption or emission maxima of C153 are observed in all the solvent systems. So, under the current experimental conditions and looking only at their steady state spectra, both the DES and hydroxyl ILs seem to be indistinguishable from each other, indicating similar polar environments for both the DES and hydroxyl ILs.

However, just by monitoring the absorption and emission spectra of C153 in the concerned solvent, it is often difficult to comprehend the medium polarity accurately. This is because the difference between the ground state and excited state dipole moments is not very high for C153 (~6 Debye).$^{58,59}$ Moreover, effects such as solute–solvent hydrogen bonding interaction are not well accounted for C153 when the polarity of a solvent is estimated through steady state spectral shift of C153.$^{58,59}$ Here, we would also like to note that many previous studies$^{29-32,59,60}$ on DESs and ionic liquids also fail to distinguish completely the medium polarity only by observing the steady state spectral properties of C153. It is not surprising as Reichardt's dye 30 is found to be insoluble in many molecular liquids, and more importantly, the long wavelength CT band also remains absent in many molecular solvents. 61 The absence of the long wavelength CT band of Reichardt's dye 30 can be explained by considering the protonation of phenolate oxygen atoms arising from the acidity of these hydroxyl ILs. 61

Considering the above discussion, we have employed elec- tron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy which proves to be an important tool and alternative to the aforementioned methods for estimating the small change in medium polarity precisely by monitoring the EPR spectra of free radical probes such as 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) in media like ionic liquids. 31,62,63 The nitroxide radical of TEMPO usually exists in a charge transfer (CT) structure and shows a triplet hyperfine structure with unequal intensities in the EPR spectra. 62-64 The nitrogen isotropic hyperfine coupling con- stant is usually described by the parameter (aN/G) with units of Gauss. The (aN/G) value usually represents the measure for perturbations of the spin-density distribution of the radicals (in our case it is TEMPO) in solution caused by electrostatic

interactions and hydrogen bonding with the solvent. It has also been reported that the value of (aN/G) depends on the spin density around the nitrogen atom. With increase in polarity of the medium, the stabilization of the ground state CT structure of the nitroxide radical increases the spin density around the nitrogen atom, which subsequently increases the (aN/G) value of TEMPO. Thus, a quantitative idea about the difference in polarity between the DES and hydroxyl ILs can be obtained by estimating the aN/G value of TEMPO in the concerned solvents. The EPR spectra of TEMPO, along with the corresponding simulated spectra, in both the DES and hydroxyl ILs are shown in Fig. 2. From Fig. 2, one can notice the difference in the line shapes of the EPR signals in all the media. Here we would like to mention that the line shape of EPR spectra usually reflects the spin relaxation process due to the tumbling motion of TEMPO radicals. 62,63 EPR spectra that differ in line shape indicate the difference in the rotational behaviour of TEMPO in these solvents. 62-64 It has been reported earlier that the rotational motion of TEMPO in a particular solvent is signifi- cantly affected by the viscosity, intermolecular hydrogen bonding interaction of TEMPO with the solvent molecule and extent of microheterogeneity of the solvent. 63,64 Since the aforementioned properties of the concerned solvent systems are different for each solvent, it is reasonable to observe a difference in the line shape of the EPR spectral signal due to a change in the microenviron- ment of these solvent systems.

Here we would like to note that for viscous and confined media like DESs and RTILs, the assessment of aN/G values from the maxima of two successive hyperfine lines may lead to imprecise estimation of the aN/G value because of spectral broadening.64 In such a scenario, the aN/G values have been estimated from the centre point of two consecutive hyperfine lines. Furthermore, Shibuya and co-workers62 suggested that the oxygen of ATEMPO (4-amino-2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl) can interact with the C2 hydrogen of 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide through hydrogen bonding interaction and thus increase the aN/G and polarity values of the medium. In light of these findings, in the present study, we can infer that in [OHEMIM][NTf2] both C2 hydrogen and the hydroxyl group can form H-bonding interaction with the anion as well as with the oxygen of the nitroxide radical and thus enhance the polarity of the medium to a greater extent as compared to those of the other two hydroxyl ILs. Here we would like to mention that the hyper-polarity of the hydroxyl ILs is one of the interesting findings as these functionalized ILs can be potential candidates for highly polar non-acidic and non-aqueous media which can be used as substitutes for water and highly polar organic solvents in synthesis and catalysis.61

As both the DES and hydroxyl ILs are viscous media, where solvation of a solute fluorophore is relatively slow as compared to common solvents such as water, DMSO, and ethanol, fluorescence can be observed from different unrelaxed states of the solvent around the fluorophore in these media.51,58 Especially, when the fluorescence lifetime of the fluorophore is much shorter than the average solvation time in a particular solvent, fluorophores may exist in a state where they are not fully solvent-equilibrated. Under this condition the micro-environments around the fluorophores are different and they show a shift in the emission maxima upon varying the wave-length of the excitation source. This is a very well-known method for determining the micro-heterogeneous behaviour of a given heterogeneous solvent.51,58,66,67 In the current studies, we have tried to explore the difference in the micro-heterogeneous behaviour of the DES and hydroxyl ILs by employing excitation wavelength (λex) dependent shift in fluorescence maxima (λemmax) of 2-amino-7-nitrofluorene (ANF). ## 3.4. Fluorescence correlation spectroscopic (FCS) studies FCS is a highly sensitive single molecule detection technique which is employed for the studies of different dynamical processes such as molecular translational diffusion, conformation fluctuations, reaction kinetics, and blinking dynamics. 74-76 Many researchers have also used FCS exclusively for the measurement of the translational diffusion of different probe molecules in DESS and RTILs, which provides information regarding the extent of solute–solvent association and the local environment of the medium. 29,52,74-78 Therefore, in the present investigation, FCS studies have also been performed to get a better understanding of the probes' diffusion dynamics and intermolecular solute–solvent interaction at a single molecular level.

Fig. 8 presents the fluorescence correlation decay curves (G(τ)) of C153 and MPTS in ethaline medium. The data have been fitted through both the single component diffusion model and anomalous diffusion model (eqn (6)). However, looking at the fit residual (as well as reduced χ²), it can be observed that the anomalous diffusion model fits the data (Fig. 8a and c) in a much better way as compared to the single component diffu- sion model (Fig. 8b and d). The normalized FCS decay curves of C153 and MPTS are provided in Fig. 8e and f respectively. The anomalous diffusion models fitting for C153 and MPTS in the hydroxyl ILs are provided in Fig. S7 and S8 (ESI†) respectively.

The stretching exponent, β, of the anomalous diffusion model represents the extent of deviation from the single component diffusion model and gives a broad distribution of diffusion times (τD) of the probe molecules. The stretching exponent β values along with the translational diffusion coefficients (Dt) of the probes in their respective solvent systems estimated from eqn (6) and (7) are shown in Table 6.

From Table 7 one can notice that the diffusion coefficient ($D_t$) of C153 is found to be much higher in ethaline as compared to that in [OHC3CH][NTf$_2$] due to the fact that the medium viscosity of the former is lower than the latter. More interestingly, for the DES ethaline, the $D_t$ value of C153 is found to be ~2.5 times higher than that for MPTS. This indicates that the frictional resistance to the translational diffusion of MPTS in ethaline is relatively more than those for MPTS in the hydroxyl ILs. ## 4. Conclusion The present study has been undertaken basically to understand the differences in microscopic behaviour in terms of intermolecular interactions, dynamics and structures between DESs and RTILs. For this purpose, a choline chloride-based DES (ethaline) and three hydroxyl functionalized ionic liquids have been employed so that, apart from the hydrogen bonding interaction, the roles of various other types of intermolecular interactions among the constituent species of the solvent systems in governing their behaviours are understood. All these investigations have unravelled several interesting findings. Excitation wavelength dependent emission spectra have indicated that the hydroxyl ILs employed in these studies are spatially more heterogeneous as compared to ethaline. EPR spectral measurements have revealed that the polarities of the hydroxyl ILs employed in this study are significantly high, whereas the polarity of ethaline is found to be close to those of aliphatic poly-hydroxy alcohols. This hyper-polarity of the hydroxyl ILs has been rationalized by considering the intramolecular synergistic effect that exists between the hydroxyl group of the cation and the corresponding anion. Investigations of the rotational and translational diffusion dynamics of selected probes have indicated that the extent of solute-solvent interaction is relatively higher in the DES in comparison to the hydroxyl ILs. Interestingly, diffusion studies have revealed that decoupling of solute dynamics with medium viscosity is found to be more for the hydroxyl ILs than that for ethaline, indicating that the extent of dynamic heterogeneity is more in the hydroxyl ILs than in ethaline. Measurements and analysis of self-diffusion coefficients through NMR have suggested that ethaline has a larger hydrodynamic radius than the hydroxyl ILs, indicating a more associated structure in ethaline. Essentially, all the results obtained from these investigations have demonstrated that despite having similar functional moieties, different intra/intermolecular interactions (such as solute-solvent interaction, specific hydrogen bonding interaction, and coulombic interaction) operating at the microscopic level are considerably different between the DES and hydroxyl ILs. This further highlights that all these interactions and energetics lead to a distribution of relaxation rates as well as spatial rearrangement which are different for the DES and hydroxyl ILs and are primarily responsible for observing the difference in the micro-heterogeneous behaviour between the DES and hydroxyl ILs. These differences in intermolecular interactions and micro-heterogeneous behaviour are manifested in the structure-property relationship for these solvent systems. Hence, the outcomes of the present study have revealed that consideration of DESs as a subclass of ILs may not be appropriate and DESs should be treated as a special class of solvent systems having its own identity.

Phys.*, 2022, 24, 7093 Choline chloride and ethylene glycol based deep eutectic solvent (DES) *versus* hydroxyl functionalized room temperature ionic liquids (RTILs): assessing the differences in microscopic behaviour between the DES and RTILs† Sahadev Barik, ID ^ab Manjari Chakraborty, ID ^ab Amita Mahapatra ID ^ab and Moloy Sarkar ID ^*ab With the aim of understanding the differences in the behavior of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) and room temperature ionic liquids (RTILs) in terms of their structure, dynamics, and intra- and intermolecular interactions, three different ILs and one DES having similar functionalities (hydroxyl) have been investigated by using both ensembled average and single-molecule spectroscopic techniques. Specifically, for this purpose, a choline chloride based DES (ethaline) and three hydroxyl functionalized ILs (1-(2-hydroxyethyl)-3-imidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHEMIM][NTF2]), N-(2-hydroxyl ethyl)-N-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHEMPY][NTf2]), and N-(2-hydroxyethyl)- N,N-dimethylpropan-1-aminium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHC3CH][NTf2])) are employed and investigated by EPR, time-resolved fluorescence, NMR and FCS studies. More interestingly, PFG-NMR measurements have indicated that the fluid structure of ethaline is relatively more associated as compared to those of the ILs despite the fact that all the cations have the same hydroxyl functionalities. All these investigations have essentially demonstrated that, despite having similar functionalities, both the DES and hydroxyl ILs employed in the present study exhibit microscopic behaviours that are significantly different from each other, indicating the interplay of various intermolecular interactions within the constituent species in governing the behaviours of these solvent systems. RTILs are salts with low melting points which entirely consist of ions and are liquids at room temperature. 1,2,12 Since there are numerous possible combinations of cations and anions, many ILs can be prepared as per the need of the end-user, and because of this, these solvents are termed 'designer solvents'. 2,12 With increase in chemical variety among ILs, they are further classified into task specific ILs, functionalized ILs, protic ILs and poly-ionic ILs. 15-17 In contrast to ILs, DESs are usually prepared by the combination of hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), which results in a significant decrease in the freezing point temperature owing to the extensive interspecies hydrogen bonding network. 7-9,18 The most common HBA are usually ammonium and phosphonium salts, whereas HBD are usually alcohols, amides and acid functionalities. 7-9 Since the starting materials for the preparation of DESs are relatively cheaper as compared to ILs, large scale preparation of DESs is possible for their use in various fields such as electrochemistry, 19,20 synthesis, 21 catalysis, 18,22 nanotechnology, 23,24 and gas adsorption. 25 Some notable experimental techniques like fluorescence, 26-32 small angle neutron scattering, 33,34 NMR diffusion 35-39 and theo- retical studies based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulation 40-45 have been used to explore the microscopic structural organisation and dynamics of DESs and RTILs independently. Atkins and co-workers 17 suggested that ILs have huge structural diversity depending on the nature of ions as well as their self- organisation into ion pairs, ions' crystal lattice, H-bonding network and micellar domains. Fayer and co-workers 46 also reported that the intra- and intermolecular interactions in ILs have significant impact on the heterogeneous microstructural organisation and liquid morphology which contribute to the dynamic heterogeneity of ILs. Moreover, the complex solvation processes of ILs have also been reported by many groups and it has been demonstrated that the multiple time scales of solvent relaxation phenomena are significantly affected by the hetero- geneity of the medium. 47-49 However, for DESs the assessment of the heterogeneity of the medium is not straightforward. For example, Biswas and co-workers 32,50,51 have reported that the non-ionic DES formed by the combination of acetamide and urea is not heterogeneous, whereas the choline chloride/urea combination or acetamide/electrolyte mixture are both spatially and dynamically heterogenous. Furthermore, the DES ethaline, a mixture of choline chloride and ethylene glycol, is reported to be spatially homogeneous but dynamically heterogeneous. 52,53 Though there are a few studies which describe the structural organisation of some neat ILs and DESs, the understanding about the differences in microscopic structural organisation between these two classes of substances still remains hazy. Therefore, it would be interesting to probe the differences in microscopic behaviour between DESs and ILs in terms of the nature of solute-solvent interaction, intermolecular interaction and dynamics of the solvent systems by employing DESs and ILs having similar functional moieties. Studies on this aspect are expected to be helpful in understanding the structure- property relationship for these classes of substances (DESs and RTILs). In light of the foregoing discussion, the current study focuses on the understanding of differences in microscopic behaviour between DESs and ionic liquids. The hydroxyl group based ILs have been chosen purposefully so that apart from the role of the hydroxyl group, various other factors which account for the microscopic behaviour of both DES and ILs can be clearly understood. Furthermore, for a fair comparison between the DES and ionic liquids, a cholinium ionic liquid ([OHC3CH][NTf2]) (Chart 1) consisting of the propyl chain has also been used for this study. The self-diffusion coefficients of all the samples were deter- mined using pulse field gradient (PFG) NMR techniques. A stimulated echo bipolar pulse-gradient pulse (stebpgp) sequence was applied with a maximum gradient pulse strength of 50 G cm⁻¹. The echo heights were attained by varying the gradient pulse strength from 2 to 95% at 16 equal intervals. The echo heights were fitted using the Stejskal–Tanner equation,⁵⁵ which is given below: S(g) = S(0) exp -Dγ^2 δ^2 g^2 (Δ - δ/3) (4) where S(g) and S(0) are the echo heights at the gradient strengths g and 0, respectively. y and δ are the gyromagnetic ratio of the proton and gradient pulse length, respectively, while Δ is the duration between the two gradient pulses. The experimental error limit for the PFG NMR diffusion experiment is ~±10%. The FCS technique is a very sensitive and powerful tool for estimating the translational diffusion (D) of a probe molecule in the concerned solvent system. This measurement was performed by placing a highly diluted sample (10-20 nM) over a coverslip which in turn was placed over the water immersion objective through which the excitation laser light was passed. The fluctuations in fluorescence intensity of the sample were measured in very small observation volumes (~1 fL) with the help of a pinhole. Now, these fluctuating fluorescence signals were detected using two SPAD detectors and were cross-correlated to generate the correlation curves G(t). The decay of the correlation function with respect to time was used for obtaining dynamical information on translational diffusion. The correlation function G(τ) of the fluorescence intensity is given by 54 G(\tau) = \frac{\langle \delta F(t) \delta F(t+\tau) \rangle}{\langle F(t)^2 \rangle} (5) where δF(t) and δF(t + τ) represent the fluctuations in fluorescence intensity around the mean value at times t and (t + τ), respectively, and F(t) is the average fluorescence intensity. The correlation data were fitted to both single-component diffusion (β = 1) and anomalous diffusion (β < 1) using the equation⁵⁶ G(τ) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{N \times \left[1 + (\tau/\tau_D)^{\beta}\right] \times \left[\sqrt{1 + (\tau/\tau_D)^{\beta}\left(\frac{1}{k^2}\right)}\right]} \end{bmatrix} (6) In eqn (6), N represents the average number of fluorescent molecules in the observation volume, τ is the delay or lag time, and τD is the translational diffusion time constant or the time taken for the fluorophore molecule to diffuse through the observation volume. β (0 < β < 1) is the stretching exponent representing the distribution of τD and k represents the aspect ratio of the observation volume which is given by k = z/wxy, where z and wxy are the longitudinal and transverse radii of the observation volume, respectively. Conclusion The present study has been undertaken basically to understand the differences in microscopic behaviour in terms of intermolecular interactions, dynamics and structures between DESs and RTILs. For this purpose, a choline chloride-based DES (ethaline) and three hydroxyl functionalized ionic liquids have been employed so that, apart from the hydrogen bonding interaction, the roles of various other types of intermolecular interactions among the constituent species of the solvent systems in governing their behaviours are understood. All these investigations have unravelled several interesting findings. Excitation wavelength dependent emission spectra have indicated that the hydroxyl ILs employed in these studies are spatially more heterogeneous as compared to ethaline. EPR spectral measurements have revealed that the polarities of the hydroxyl ILs employed in this study are significantly high, whereas the polarity of ethaline is found to be close to those of aliphatic poly-hydroxy alcohols. This hyper-polarity of the hydroxyl ILs has been rationalized by considering the intramolecular synergistic effect that exists between the hydroxyl group of the cation and the corresponding anion. Investigations of the rotational and translational diffusion dynamics of selected probes have indicated that the extent of solute-solvent interaction is relatively higher in the DES in comparison to the hydroxyl ILs. Interestingly, diffusion studies have revealed that decoupling of solute dynamics with medium viscosity is found to be more for the hydroxyl ILs than that for ethaline, indicating that the extent of dynamic heterogeneity is more in the hydroxyl ILs than in ethaline. Measurements and analysis of self-diffusion coefficients through NMR have suggested that ethaline has a larger hydrodynamic radius than the hydroxyl ILs, indicating a more associated structure in ethaline. Essentially, all the results obtained from these investigations have demonstrated that despite having similar functional moieties, different intra/intermolecular interactions (such as solute-solvent interaction, specific hydrogen bonding interaction, and coulombic interaction) operating at the microscopic level are considerably different between the DES and hydroxyl ILs. This further highlights that all these interactions and energetics lead to a distribution of relaxation rates as well as spatial rearrangement which are different for the DES and hydroxyl ILs and are primarily responsible for observing the difference in the micro-heterogeneous behaviour between the DES and hydroxyl ILs. These differences in intermolecular interactions and micro-heterogeneous behaviour are manifested in the structure-property relationship for these solvent systems. Hence, the outcomes of the present study have revealed that consideration of DESs as a subclass of ILs may not be appropriate and DESs should be treated as a special class of solvent systems having its own identity. Phys.*, 2022, 24, 7093 Choline chloride and ethylene glycol based deep eutectic solvent (DES) *versus* hydroxyl functionalized room temperature ionic liquids (RTILs): assessing the differences in microscopic behaviour between the DES and RTILs† Sahadev Barik, ID ^ab Manjari Chakraborty, ID ^ab Amita Mahapatra ID ^ab and Moloy Sarkar ID ^*ab With the aim of understanding the differences in the behavior of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) and room temperature ionic liquids (RTILs) in terms of their structure, dynamics, and intra- and intermolecular interactions, three different ILs and one DES having similar functionalities (hydroxyl) have been investigated by using both ensembled average and single-molecule spectroscopic techniques. Specifically, for this purpose, a choline chloride based DES (ethaline) and three hydroxyl functionalized ILs (1-(2-hydroxyethyl)-3-imidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHEMIM][NTF2]), N-(2-hydroxyl ethyl)-N-methylpyrrolidinium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHEMPY][NTf2]), and N-(2-hydroxyethyl)- N,N-dimethylpropan-1-aminium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([OHC3CH][NTf2])) are employed and investigated by EPR, time-resolved fluorescence, NMR and FCS studies. Estimation of polarity through EPR spectroscopy has revealed that the hydroxyl ILs employed in these studies are hyper-polar (close to water) in nature, whereas the polarity of the DES is found to be close to those of aliphatic polyhydroxy-alcohols. Interestingly, both time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy and FCS studies on these systems have suggested that the hydroxyl ILs are more dynamically heterogeneous than the DES. More interestingly, PFG-NMR measurements have indicated that the fluid structure of ethaline is relatively more associated as compared to those of the ILs despite the fact that all the cations have the same hydroxyl functionalities. All these investigations have essentially demonstrated that, despite having similar functionalities, both the DES and hydroxyl ILs employed in the present study exhibit microscopic behaviours that are significantly different from each other, indicating the interplay of various intermolecular interactions within the constituent species in governing the behaviours of these solvent systems. RTILs are salts with low melting points which entirely consist of ions and are liquids at room temperature. 1,2,12 Since there are numerous possible combinations of cations and anions, many ILs can be prepared as per the need of the end-user, and because of this, these solvents are termed 'designer solvents'. 2,12 With increase in chemical variety among ILs, they are further classified into task specific ILs, functionalized ILs, protic ILs and poly-ionic ILs. 15-17 In contrast to ILs, DESs are usually prepared by the combination of hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), which results in a significant decrease in the freezing point temperature owing to the extensive interspecies hydrogen bonding network. 7-9,18 The most common HBA are usually ammonium and phosphonium salts, whereas HBD are usually alcohols, amides and acid functionalities. 7-9 Since the starting materials for the preparation of DESs are relatively cheaper as compared to ILs, large scale preparation of DESs is possible for their use in various fields such as electrochemistry, 19,20 synthesis, 21 catalysis, 18,22 nanotechnology, 23,24 and gas adsorption. 25 Some notable experimental techniques like fluorescence, 26-32 small angle neutron scattering, 33,34 NMR diffusion 35-39 and theo- retical studies based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulation 40-45 have been used to explore the microscopic structural organisation and dynamics of DESs and RTILs independently. Atkins and co-workers 17 suggested that ILs have huge structural diversity depending on the nature of ions as well as their self- organisation into ion pairs, ions' crystal lattice, H-bonding network and micellar domains. Fayer and co-workers 46 also reported that the intra- and intermolecular interactions in ILs have significant impact on the heterogeneous microstructural organisation and liquid morphology which contribute to the dynamic heterogeneity of ILs. Moreover, the complex solvation processes of ILs have also been reported by many groups and it has been demonstrated that the multiple time scales of solvent relaxation phenomena are significantly affected by the hetero- geneity of the medium. 47-49 However, for DESs the assessment of the heterogeneity of the medium is not straightforward. For example, Biswas and co-workers 32,50,51 have reported that the non-ionic DES formed by the combination of acetamide and urea is not heterogeneous, whereas the choline chloride/urea combination or acetamide/electrolyte mixture are both spatially and dynamically heterogenous. Furthermore, the DES ethaline, a mixture of choline chloride and ethylene glycol, is reported to be spatially homogeneous but dynamically heterogeneous. 52,53 Though there are a few studies which describe the structural organisation of some neat ILs and DESs, the understanding about the differences in microscopic structural organisation between these two classes of substances still remains hazy. Therefore, it would be interesting to probe the differences in microscopic behaviour between DESs and ILs in terms of the nature of solute-solvent interaction, intermolecular interaction and dynamics of the solvent systems by employing DESs and ILs having similar functional moieties. Studies on this aspect are expected to be helpful in understanding the structure- property relationship for these classes of substances (DESs and RTILs). In light of the foregoing discussion, the current study focuses on the understanding of differences in microscopic behaviour between DESs and ionic liquids. For this purpose, a DES, namely ethaline (choline chloride + ethylene glycol 1:2 ratio), and three other hydroxyl group containing room temperature ionic liquids are employed for the study. The hydroxyl group based ILs have been chosen purposefully so that apart from the role of the hydroxyl group, various other factors which account for the microscopic behaviour of both DES and ILs can be clearly understood. Furthermore, for a fair comparison between the DES and ionic liquids, a cholinium ionic liquid ([OHC3CH][NTf2]) (Chart 1) consisting of the propyl chain has also been used for this study. The differences in microscopic behaviour between the DES and hydroxyl ILs have been investigated with the help of different spectroscopic techniques such as steady state and time resolved fluorescence spectroscopy, fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy so that information regarding the local environment, the solute-solvent interaction and the dynamics of the solvent systems can be obtained. Experimental ### 2.1. Materials Ethylene glycol, 1-methylimidazole, N-methylpyrrolidine, N,N-dimethylethanolamine, 1-bromopropane, Coumarin (153), perylene, 8-methoxypyrene-1,3,6-trisulfonic acid trisodium salt (MPTS), and 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Instrumentation The absorption spectra of the samples were collected using a Cary 100 biospectrophotometer. A Cary Eclipse fluorescence (Agilent Technologies) spectrophotometer was used for recording the steady state fluorescence spectra of the samples. A time correlated single photon counting (TCSPC) spectrometer (OB 920) was used for the measurements of time resolved fluorescence anisotropy with the help of a 405 nm picosecond diode laser (EPL) as an excitation source. A dilute solution of Ludox in water was taken as a scatterer to obtain the instrument response function (IRF) and it was found to be around 80 ps for the 405 nm laser. Fluorescence intensities for parallel (||) and perpendicular (⊥) polarization were collected alternatively until a peak difference between the parallel (||) and perpendicular (⊥) decays of ~5000 (at _t_ = 0) was observed. The same procedure was applied for _G_-factor calculation but with horizontal polarization of the exciting laser beam and 5 cycles of repetition. The temperature of the cell was monitored by circulating water through the cell holder using a Quantum along with a North West (TC 125) temperature controller. A Hamamatsu microchannel plate photomultiplier tube (R3809U-50) detector was used to collect the decay signals of the samples. The decay curves were analysed with the help of F980 decay analysis software. The decay curves were fitted through non-linear least squares iteration methods and the quality of the fitting was judged from the chi-square (x²) values as well as by verifying the weight deviation. The viscosities of all the samples were measured using an LVDV-III Ultra Brookfield Cone and Plate viscometer (experimental error: ±2%). A Bruker Super QCW-EPR bridge (model A300) X band spectrometer was used for recording the EPR spectra and WinEPR SymFonia software (version 1.26 beta) was used for simulation of the EPR spectra. All the NMR measurements were carried out on a 9.4 T Bruker Avance NMR spectrometer with 400.1 MHz Larmor frequencies for H¹. For FCS measurements, a time-resolved confocal fluores-cence setup (MicroTime 200, PicoQuant), equipped with an inverted microscope (Olympus IX 71) along with a water immersion objective (Olympus UPlanSApo NA 1.2, 60x), was used. The excitation source was a pulsed diode laser (403 nm) with an FWHM of 176 ps and a repetition rate of 20 MHz. The laser beam was made to pass through a polarization maintain-ing single-mode optical fiber and focused onto the sample (which was placed on a coverslip) using a water immersion objective which was also used to collect the fluorescence light emitted from the samples. The emitted beam was then filtered by using a 425 nm filter to remove any excitation light. The signal was then focused onto a 50 µm diameter pinhole to remove the out-of-focus signal, recollimated, and directed onto a (50/50) beam splitter prior to entering two single-photon avalanche photodiodes (SPADs). The signals from the two SPAD detectors were cross-correlated to generate fluorescence corre-lation traces. A SymPhoTime software controlled PicoHarp300 TCSPC module was used for data acquisition in a time-tagged time-resolved (TTTR) mode. All FCS experiments were carried out at room temperature (~298 K). During all FCS measure-ments, the excitation power was kept at ~4 µW. The excitation power was kept low during all FCS studies so as to avoid the contribution of background noise. The anisotropy data were fitted to calculate the rotational relaxation time by the following equation: $r(t) = r_0e^{(-t/τ_r)}$ (3) where $r_0$ is the initial anisotropy and $\tau_r$ is the rotational relaxation time. The self-diffusion coefficients of all the samples were deter- mined using pulse field gradient (PFG) NMR techniques. A stimulated echo bipolar pulse-gradient pulse (stebpgp) sequence was applied with a maximum gradient pulse strength of 50 G cm⁻¹. The echo heights were attained by varying the gradient pulse strength from 2 to 95% at 16 equal intervals. The echo heights were fitted using the Stejskal–Tanner equation,⁵⁵ which is given below: S(g) = S(0) exp -Dγ^2 δ^2 g^2 (Δ - δ/3) (4) where S(g) and S(0) are the echo heights at the gradient strengths g and 0, respectively. y and δ are the gyromagnetic ratio of the proton and gradient pulse length, respectively, while Δ is the duration between the two gradient pulses. The experimental error limit for the PFG NMR diffusion experiment is ~±10%. The FCS technique is a very sensitive and powerful tool for estimating the translational diffusion (D) of a probe molecule in the concerned solvent system. This measurement was performed by placing a highly diluted sample (10-20 nM) over a coverslip which in turn was placed over the water immersion objective through which the excitation laser light was passed. The fluctuations in fluorescence intensity of the sample were measured in very small observation volumes (~1 fL) with the help of a pinhole. Now, these fluctuating fluorescence signals were detected using two SPAD detectors and were cross-correlated to generate the correlation curves G(t). The decay of the correlation function with respect to time was used for obtaining dynamical information on translational diffusion. The correlation function G(τ) of the fluorescence intensity is given by 54 G(\tau) = \frac{\langle \delta F(t) \delta F(t+\tau) \rangle}{\langle F(t)^2 \rangle} (5) where δF(t) and δF(t + τ) represent the fluctuations in fluorescence intensity around the mean value at times t and (t + τ), respectively, and F(t) is the average fluorescence intensity. The correlation data were fitted to both single-component diffusion (β = 1) and anomalous diffusion (β < 1) using the equation⁵⁶ G(τ) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{N \times \left[1 + (\tau/\tau_D)^{\beta}\right] \times \left[\sqrt{1 + (\tau/\tau_D)^{\beta}\left(\frac{1}{k^2}\right)}\right]} \end{bmatrix} (6) In eqn (6), N represents the average number of fluorescent molecules in the observation volume, τ is the delay or lag time, and τD is the translational diffusion time constant or the time taken for the fluorophore molecule to diffuse through the observation volume. β (0 < β < 1) is the stretching exponent representing the distribution of τD and k represents the aspect ratio of the observation volume which is given by k = z/wxy, where z and wxy are the longitudinal and transverse radii of the observation volume, respectively. The excitation volume of the FCS setup was calibrated by taking a dilute solution of Rhodamine 6G (R6G) in water whose translational diffusion coefficient (Dt) is 426 µm² s⁻¹.⁵⁷ The estimated excitation volume was ~0.45 fL for 405 nm laser sources. The Dt value was calculated by using eqn (7) which is provided below: D_t = \frac{w_{xy}^2}{4\tau_D} (7) ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Conclusion The present study has been undertaken basically to understand the differences in microscopic behaviour in terms of intermolecular interactions, dynamics and structures between DESs and RTILs. For this purpose, a choline chloride-based DES (ethaline) and three hydroxyl functionalized ionic liquids have been employed so that, apart from the hydrogen bonding interaction, the roles of various other types of intermolecular interactions among the constituent species of the solvent systems in governing their behaviours are understood. All these investigations have unravelled several interesting findings. Excitation wavelength dependent emission spectra have indicated that the hydroxyl ILs employed in these studies are spatially more heterogeneous as compared to ethaline. EPR spectral measurements have revealed that the polarities of the hydroxyl ILs employed in this study are significantly high, whereas the polarity of ethaline is found to be close to those of aliphatic poly-hydroxy alcohols. This hyper-polarity of the hydroxyl ILs has been rationalized by considering the intramolecular synergistic effect that exists between the hydroxyl group of the cation and the corresponding anion. Investigations of the rotational and translational diffusion dynamics of selected probes have indicated that the extent of solute-solvent interaction is relatively higher in the DES in comparison to the hydroxyl ILs. Interestingly, diffusion studies have revealed that decoupling of solute dynamics with medium viscosity is found to be more for the hydroxyl ILs than that for ethaline, indicating that the extent of dynamic heterogeneity is more in the hydroxyl ILs than in ethaline. Measurements and analysis of self-diffusion coefficients through NMR have suggested that ethaline has a larger hydrodynamic radius than the hydroxyl ILs, indicating a more associated structure in ethaline. Essentially, all the results obtained from these investigations have demonstrated that despite having similar functional moieties, different intra/intermolecular interactions (such as solute-solvent interaction, specific hydrogen bonding interaction, and coulombic interaction) operating at the microscopic level are considerably different between the DES and hydroxyl ILs. This further highlights that all these interactions and energetics lead to a distribution of relaxation rates as well as spatial rearrangement which are different for the DES and hydroxyl ILs and are primarily responsible for observing the difference in the micro-heterogeneous behaviour between the DES and hydroxyl ILs. These differences in intermolecular interactions and micro-heterogeneous behaviour are manifested in the structure-property relationship for these solvent systems. Hence, the outcomes of the present study have revealed that consideration of DESs as a subclass of ILs may not be appropriate and DESs should be treated as a special class of solvent systems having its own identity.
